89	### Keep child branches linear — it decides how painful the merge is
90	
91	When a parent branch gains commits after its child was cut, **rebase the child onto the parent** (the child is unpushed or yours alone) rather than merging the parent in. Stack 03 learned this the expensive way; see below.
92	
93	### Merging a stack — what actually happens (learned 2026-09-17, twice)
94	
95	**`gh pr merge` refuses a stacked pull request**, and on the top of a stack it silently merges into the parent branch instead of `main`. Never use it on a stack. Merge **bottom-up** through the async route; `plans/scripts/land.sh <pr> "<title>" <message-file>` does the waiting and polling:
96	
97	```bash
98	gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async -f merge_method=squash \
99	  -f commit_title="<subject> (#<n>)" -f commit_message="<the What, as prose>" -f sha=<head sha>
100	gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/<n>/merge-async/<uuid>      # poll until "merged"
101	```
102	
103	After a parent merges:
104	
105	1. **A linear child is restacked by GitHub itself** within about half a minute: rebased onto `main`, base retargeted to `main`. Your local copy of that branch is now behind a rewritten remote — check the trees are identical (`git diff --quiet origin/<b> <b>`) and `git reset --hard origin/<b>`. Then wait for checks and merge.
106	2. **A child carrying merge commits is not restacked.** Two cases:
107	   - *It is a strict superset of `main`* (it merged its parents in as they were first written). Prove it — the merged pull requests' original tips are ancestors, and `git diff --stat origin/main HEAD` lists only this pull request's files. A plain `git merge origin/main` will conflict on every file both sides touched (add/add against the squashed copies), so record the merge with `git merge -s ours origin/main`, confirm the tree did not change, push, `gh pr edit <n> --base main`.

148	## 8. Lessons — read these twice
149	
150	1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
151	2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
152	3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
153	4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
154	5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
155	6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
156	7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
157	8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
158	9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
159	10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
160	11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
161	12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
162	13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
163	15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
164	16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
165	17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
166	18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
167	14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

1	#!/bin/bash
2	# land.sh <pr> <title> <message-file>
3	# GitHub restacks a child branch onto main by itself when its parent merges, so this only:
4	# checks the base is main and the branch sits on main, waits for the four checks, squash-merges via the async route.
5	set -euo pipefail
6	PR=$1; TITLE=$2; MSG=$3
7	cd /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst
8	for i in $(seq 1 12); do BASE=$(gh pr view $PR --json baseRefName -q .baseRefName); [ "$BASE" = "main" ] && break; sleep 5; done
9	[ "$BASE" = "main" ] || { echo "base is $BASE, not main"; exit 3; }
10	git fetch -q origin
11	HEAD_SHA=$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)
12	git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main $HEAD_SHA || { echo "head $HEAD_SHA does not sit on main yet"; exit 5; }
13	echo "head ${HEAD_SHA:0:7} sits on main; waiting for checks…"
14	for i in $(seq 1 90); do
15	  out=$(gh pr checks $PR 2>&1 || true)
16	  if echo "$out" | grep -qw "fail"; then echo "CHECK FAILED:"; echo "$out"; exit 4; fi
17	  if ! echo "$out" | grep -qw "pending" && [ "$(echo "$out" | grep -cw pass)" -ge 4 ]; then break; fi
18	  sleep 10
19	done
20	gh pr checks $PR | awk '{print $1"="$2}' | tr '\n' ' '; echo
21	[ "$(gh pr view $PR --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid)" = "$HEAD_SHA" ] || { echo "head moved while waiting"; exit 6; }
22	R=$(gh api -X PUT repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/$PR/merge-async -f merge_method=squash -f commit_title="$TITLE (#$PR)" -f commit_message="$(cat "$MSG")" -f sha=$HEAD_SHA)
23	UUID=$(echo "$R" | jq -r .details.uuid)
24	for i in $(seq 1 30); do r=$(gh api repos/kgang/katalyst/pulls/$PR/merge-async/$UUID); [ "$(echo "$r" | jq -r .status)" != "pending" ] && break; sleep 5; done
25	echo "$r" | jq -c .

66	    seed: int                           # what domain/ will propagate with

70

109	    reason: Literal["reached_terminal", "depth_cap", "width_cap", "claim_cap",
110	                    "spend_cap", "refusal_cap", "no_terminal"]
111	                                        # ONE RULE (proposals.md B4): the reason names what closed the LAST open claim —
112	                                        # an ending or a Stop -> reached_terminal; a cap -> that cap (three refusals in a
113	                                        # row is the refusal cap; it was "model_stopped", but the model did not stop);
114	                                        # spend_cap and no_terminal override
115	                                        # no "search_cap": reaching the search cap stops SEARCHING, not the
116	                                        # generation (later arrows are `argued`), so it is never a stop reason
117	                                        # why the GENERATION stopped. "no_path" is on Verdict only (S3)

126	**The transport is `POST /api/generate` read as a stream, not `EventSource`** (*decided here*). Two reasons, both hard: the request carries a hypothesis, an optional target, an optional user belief and a seed, and `EventSource` can only send a GET with no body; and `EventSource` reconnects by itself, which would silently re-run a generation and spend the money twice. The browser uses `fetch` and reads the body. The wire format is still server-sent events — `event:` and `data:` lines — so the format stays inspectable in a terminal with `curl`.
127	
128	**Four things the cross-chapter review settled (2026-09-17), binding on both stacks.** (1) **A `Stop` and a closed claim make no event of their own.** A `Stop` leaves a transcript line; the next growth event's `frontier` no longer names that claim, and on `beliefs_propagated` **every skeleton goes** — the frontier is empty by definition — so no rectangle ever stands where nothing will arrive. (2) **Which recording plays:** the replayer matches the request's `hypothesis` against each recording's `generation_started.hypothesis`, exact after trimming surrounding spaces; nothing matches → one plain sentence, never a guess. (3) **Readiness says what can be replayed:** `Readiness.replayable: tuple[RecordingSummary, ...]`, `RecordingSummary{example: str, recording_date: date}` — one name, `recording_date`, everywhere. (4) **Anything that is not an accepted proposal counts toward the three in a row** — a validator rejection, a vendor refusal, a malformed answer — one rule, not three.
129	
130	**A recording is this same stream, line for line** — `backend/recordings/<example>.jsonl`, one JSON object per line, in order, with a header line carrying the base map, the seed, the date and the prompt hash (record 0012). On replay every event is re-emitted unchanged **except two (S4)**: `receipt` is **rebuilt** with `mode: "replay"`, zero dollars, and the recording's date and hash; and `beliefs_propagated` is **recomputed** — the recording carries the seed, `domain/` re-propagates, and **a recording therefore holds no `World` at all**, which keeps the file small and makes replay and live agree by construction. Record 0012 names only four event types; the chapter must say all eight and say this.

#!/bin/bash
# heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>
#
# The one queue for anything heavy on this machine: a whole test suite, a browser
# run, a repeat bar. It waits its turn, runs the command, and gives the turn back.
# One at a time, whoever asks. Last session three or four suites ran together, the
# load sat at 20-23, and the load itself caused "flaky" failures that then had to
# be chased (STATUS 2026-09-21).
#
# The turn is a directory (making one is atomic). It holds the owner's process id,
# so a turn left behind by a killed run is taken back rather than waited on for ever.
#
# NOT for a single test file, a linter or a type check: run those directly.
set -uo pipefail
LOCK=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.lock
LOG=/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/.heavy.log
LABEL=${1:?usage: heavy.sh <label> -- <command...>}; shift
[ "${1:-}" = "--" ] && shift
waited=0
until mkdir "$LOCK" 2>/dev/null; do
  owner=$(cat "$LOCK/pid" 2>/dev/null || echo "")
  if [ -n "$owner" ] && ! kill -0 "$owner" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "heavy: taking back a turn left by dead process $owner ($(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null))" >&2
    rm -rf "$LOCK"; continue
  fi
  [ $((waited % 60)) -eq 0 ] && echo "heavy: '$LABEL' waiting behind '$(cat "$LOCK/label" 2>/dev/null)' (${waited}s)" >&2
  sleep 5; waited=$((waited + 5))
done
echo $$ > "$LOCK/pid"; echo "$LABEL" > "$LOCK/label"
trap 'rm -rf "$LOCK"' EXIT
start=$(date +%s)
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') START $LABEL (waited ${waited}s, load $(sysctl -n vm.loadavg | awk '{print $2}'))" >> "$LOG"
"$@"; code=$?
echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') END   $LABEL exit=$code took=$(( $(date +%s) - start ))s" >> "$LOG"
exit $code

# Finishing stack 04 — what every agent in this session reads second

**Read `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/briefs/04-common.md` first, fully.** It is binding: who Kent is, his two vetoes, the house rules, the report format. This page adds only what is new on 2026-09-21.

## Where the stack stands

Ten pull requests of stack 04 are on `main` (`48eb562`). Four branches remain, each in its own worktree under `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/`. The whole picture is in `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/RESUME-stack-04.md` — read the part about your branch. Kent's instruction for all of it, in his words: *"Aim for a principled but simple as possible project to understand and maintain."* When two designs both work, take the one a stranger could read fastest. Remove rather than guard. One rule over two.

## The machine is shared — the resource rules

Last session three or four agents ran whole suites and 40-times repeat runs together. The load sat at 20–23, everything slowed down, and the load itself caused "flaky" failures that then had to be chased. So:

- **Run directly, as often as you like:** one test file or a few (`uv run pytest tests/unit/domain/test_diff.py`, `npx vitest run src/stream`), the linters, the type checkers, a short script of your own.
- **A whole suite (`uv run pytest`, `npm run check`, `make test`) goes through the one queue, and at most twice in your whole task:**
  `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/scripts/heavy.sh "<your letter>: <what>" -- <command>`
  It waits its turn — possibly half an hour, behind a long browser run. **Start it in the background** and carry on; do not sit in a call that will time out.
- **Never, in any form:** `npx playwright test`, `--repeat-each`, a cold-run loop, a dev server left running, `make eval`, `make record-demo`, `make record-cassettes`. The coordinator runs every browser end-to-end run, every repeat bar, and everything that costs money, one at a time. If your work needs one, say exactly which command in your report.
- Do not start anything on ports 8015, 5187, 8071 or 5171.

## Four lessons this stack paid for (HANDOFF §8, 15–18)

- A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.
- Test a program as a program; anything paid for is kept as it goes.
- **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Five times in this stack "flaky" was a real defect a reader could hit. And pytest truncates a repr: `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`.
- Never edit a source file under somebody else's running server; never trust an end-to-end number from shared ports.

## Your report

The format in `04-common.md`, plus one line at the top: **what the coordinator must run to check you** — the exact commands, in order.

1	# Midpoint review: finish the reasoning loop and simplify its mathematics
2	
3	**Date:** 2026-09-21. **Status:** recommendation for Kent's review; no product code or accepted decisions changed.
4	
5	## Recommendation
6	
7	Keep the workbench, evidence Inspector, immutable branches, comparison, typed API, and pure domain boundary. Rebuild the quantitative contract around **small explicit models and conditional trade theses**. Finish one complete, keyless Hormuz journey before extending simulation, refinement, probes, or market coverage.
8	
9	The project's central idea fits the assignment well. Its engineering discipline is substantial. The main problem is that the mathematics and feature requirements have grown beyond the evidence supporting them, while the final thesis/strategy experience remains unfinished. Some issues are actual calculation defects, not matters of taste or insufficient disclaimers.
10	
11	Kent's stated priorities during this review were: **no fixed deadline; a compelling, complete demo with defensible assumptions; reconsider the quantitative design from the ground up when it adds apparent certainty rather than useful information.** This proposal follows those priorities. It recommends a bounded redesign, with a specific completion gate, rather than a broad research program.
12	
13	## How the independent review was conducted
14	
15	Four assignment-first passes were frozen before reading the initial brainstorming or existing design. They covered product, probability/causality, finance, and the primary reviewer's synthesis. Each subsequent audit began with `docs/initial-brainstorming.md`, then examined the specs, decisions, implementation, and history. External research used selected primary literature and the assignment's named inspiration sources.
16	
17	Three parallel reviewers used `gpt-5.6-sol`, the available successor to the requested but unavailable `gpt-5-sol`. Their findings were checked and reconciled; the final recommendation below is a synthesis, not a vote or concatenation of reports.
18	
19	The implementation review distinguishes merged `main` (`0df6c23`) from the unmerged browser (`3433266` plus dirty changes), generation (`8261053` plus dirty changes), and observation-fix (`6ee387c` plus a dirty test) worktrees. The newer work already implements much of generation and engine–canvas integration. Recommendations account for it. These are working-tree snapshots, not a claim about the current status of remote pull requests.
20	
21	## What the assignment should make central
22	
23	The brief asks for two entry points into one useful loop:
24	
25	1. Test whether a proposed event plausibly leads to a financial conclusion.
26	2. Discover tradable downstream consequences of an event.
27	
28	Both should lead through **mechanism → evidence → changed scenario → comparison → thesis**. A successful demonstration lets a reviewer explain why the trade looked interesting, what could overturn it, and what the tool still does not know.
29	
30	The brief does not require a universal causal simulator, calibrated forecasts for arbitrary events, daily price paths, portfolio risk, execution, or an ontology framework. Those are possible future directions. They should not determine the first complete product's architecture.
31	
32	## The five highest-leverage adjustments
33	
34	| Priority | Adjustment | Why it earns its cost |
35	|---|---|---|
36	| 1 | Replace the quantitative semantics for the showcase with a bounded, auditable model | Fixes actual probabilistic errors and reduces conceptual machinery |
37	| 2 | Build the conditional thesis and export next, including compatible market comparisons | Completes the assignment and prevents false trade signals |
38	| 3 | Attach evidence to the precise claim or parameter it supports | Makes auditability substantive rather than a count of citations |
39	| 4 | Integrate the existing branches and make one reviewed replay mandatory | Converts substantial unfinished work into a dependable reviewer experience |
40	| 5 | Evaluate semantic quality and time to useful output | Directs future work toward better reasoning and usability, rather than more graph structure |
41	
42	These changes reinforce one another. A smaller model needs fewer parameters to defend, fewer generated claims to research, fewer UI states to explain, and a smaller acceptance suite. The saved effort goes into the thesis and evidence.
43	
44	## Why the numerical reset is warranted
45	
46	### Observation is mathematically wrong in a tiny case
47	
48	Let `P(A)=0.20`, `P(B|A)=0.90`, and `P(B|not A)=0.10`. Observing B should yield `P(A|B)=9/13`, approximately 69%. The current engine returns 20%, unchanged. It selects simulated worlds by their realized outcomes but then averages a conditional probability that is constant for A. The full passing suite does not catch this. The primary reviewer independently reproduced the result.
49	
50	The uncommitted observation test adds another warning sign: it requires movement across a zero-strength arrow, where the declared independent model implies no update. Finite sampling noise has become expected behavior. Details and reproduction: [probability audit](06-probability-audit.md).
51	
52	### The event semantics alter the requested scenario
53	
54	The brief's “Hormuz opens, then Iran is struck” permits both events to occur. A later strike can reduce sustained shipping, increase the risk premium, or reverse the financial conclusion. It does not erase the opening event. Current automatic retraction conflates an event with a continuing state. The implementation can even retract an assumption when a newly inserted opposing source has essentially zero probability, because retraction uses its structural schedule rather than its realized truth.
55	
56	Use distinct dated claims: opening occurred; strike occurred; shipping remains usable through a later date. This makes the story and its arithmetic easier to understand.
57	
58	### Path products and uncertainty bands overstate what is known
59	
60	The Verify path product multiplies dependent marginal probabilities. If Y always equals X and both have probability 0.5, the product is 0.25 while the conjunction is 0.5. The product is neither a general joint probability nor a conservative bound. Remove it.
61	
62	The nested simulation samples a distribution fitted to model-stated probability ranges while holding important parameters and structure fixed. That can explore a declared mathematical distribution, but it does not add evidence. The variance correction does not generally recover its advertised quantiles. A later Brier score on a binary outcome cannot validate an interval over that event's latent probability; the event resolves to true or false, not to its probability.
63	
64	The literature supports distinguishing these objects. Proper scores assess specified predictive quantities; numerical outcome intervals and intervals over unknown probability parameters need different validation designs. [Gneiting and Raftery, 2007](https://doi.org/10.1198/016214506000001437). The audit also identifies mistaken transfers from FermiEval, QuantSightBench, and the forecast-consistency literature into the current ADR rationale.
65	
66	## The proposed quantitative contract
67	
68	**The broad map is a set of causal hypotheses. Quantify a small, complete portion only when doing so helps answer a decision question.**
69	
70	For the showcase, use a small acyclic graph of dated binary claims, normally with at most two direct causes per claim. Record an explicit conditional probability for each parent combination. Compute by exact enumeration at an initial cap near twelve numerical variables. No daily stochastic process, nested Monte Carlo, automatic retraction, or path product is required.
71	
72	The causal interpretation remains an assumption: the selected parents and mechanisms must be adequate for the proposed intervention. Exact arithmetic cannot identify real-world effects from generated text. [Pearl, causal intervention semantics](https://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/BOOK-2K/ch3-3.pdf).
73	
74	Show model-implied probabilities, endpoint changes, and results under a few named coherent assumption sets. The spread across those sets is a sensitivity envelope over what was tested. It has no automatic 80% coverage interpretation. Store user assumptions separately from the model's, and let the user explicitly choose which assumption set a calculation uses; never blend owners silently.
75	
76	An unquantified dependency blocks numerical propagation through it. It may still have a useful mechanism explanation. Reachability tells us which claims may be affected; it does not by itself determine direction or magnitude. Any qualitative change needs an explicit local rule with its conditions, and conflicting or incomplete rules yield ambiguity. Do not hide a model-generated revision behind a deterministic-looking animation.
77

81

# Digesting the two midpoint reviews — what every digest agent reads first

**You are one of four read-only Opus analysts.** Two independent reviews of the Katalyst project were written on 2026-09-21 by other tools: `plans/review/` (three GPT reviewers and a synthesis) and `plans/review2/` (eight Opus passes and a synthesis; it ran the app and wrote runnable reproductions). Your job is to digest the part named in your own brief, check it against the code AS IT IS TODAY, and recommend what to do — for the unfinished tail of stack 04 and above all for stacks 05, 06 and 07.

You change NO file in the repository or any worktree and run no git command that changes anything. You write exactly one report, to the path your brief names under `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/analysis/`, plus throwaway scripts under the scratch directory your brief names. Your final message is a 300-word summary of that report.

## What Kent asked for, in his words (2026-09-21)

*"read and digest the critical reviews … and make principled adjustments to the remaining portions, in particular stack 5-7. Rewrites or refactors of the previous stacks are allowed but should be weighed against a high standard of quality improvement. Try to find the best tradeoffs in terms of work required versus improvements made … Aim for a code architecture and design that is principled and simple as possible to understand and maintain."*

So the bar for touching merged work is HIGH, and the currency is improvement per unit of work. A recommendation with no cost beside it is not a recommendation. "Simple" means a stranger reads it fastest: fewer concepts, one rule over two, remove rather than guard.

## Read, in this order

1. `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/ASSIGNMENT.md` — the brief. Everything is judged against it.
2. `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/review2/00-final-proposal.md` and `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/review/00-final-proposal.md` — both recommendations, whole.

Today `main` = `48eb562` with #29–#40 merged: the engine–canvas join, the model pipeline, the event stream and replay, two locality fixes (#38), the observe-direction fix (#29). **Every finding must be re-checked against today's code before it counts** — by reading the code, or by a small script. 6. **What you did not check** — honestly.

What is the best trade between work and improvement? Evaluate AT LEAST these, each with an honest cost (sessions, lines added and deleted, which tests and chapters die, what risk) and an honest account of what it fixes and what it leaves:

(5) **"no document contains a number the engine computes"** — from the engine's side, what would make that rule cheap (a command that prints every worked number; doctest-style checks)?

Prototype if it sharpens a cost estimate — small scripts under `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/b70a1857-a894-4bbe-b3a6-4d7cf3ebc4f8/scratchpad/digest/engine/`, run with `uv run --no-sync python` from `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend`. input.prompt:
You are digest analyst FINANCE. Read `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/briefs/05-review-digest-common.md` first, fully — it is your brief's first half and it binds you. Your lens: **stack 05, the thesis — how the map becomes something a trader can act on.** Not one line of it exists yet, so unlike the other analysts you are designing on open ground: the cheapest moment to get it right.

YOUR READING (beyond the common list): `plans/review2/audit-E-finance-thesis.md`, `plans/review2/research-B-quant-finance.md`, `plans/review2/03-engine-and-finance-design.md` §2–§3 (Quantity terminals and Impact edges, price paths, the Position lens with first-touch stop and target, the inverse query by lift, shocks, priced-in and edge, sizing, the thesis card); `plans/review/07-finance-audit.md`, `plans/review/03-independent-finance.md`, `plans/review/09-worked-quantitative-alternative.md` (its conditional-versus-unconditional trade example), `plans/review/10-proposed-change-plan.md` (the thesis parts). Then what exists today: `spec/thesis/README.md` (a landing page only), decision records 0010 (grounding sources: Polymarket and FRED) and 0013 (a payoff names the trade; a quote names the price), `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` — every FR and invariant about the thesis, the stop-loss (INV-14), tails, market beliefs, export; `backend/src/katalyst/domain/proposition.py` (`ContractPayoff`, `PricePayoff`), `backend/src/katalyst/fixtures/hormuz.py` (the endings M1, M2 and what they name), `backend/src/katalyst/grounding/` (an empty package), and the present plan for stack 05 in `plans/roadmap-03-to-06.md`.

READ THE BRIEF'S WORDS CLOSELY (`ASSIGNMENT.md`): which clauses actually need a POSITION (an instrument, a side, an entry, a stop, a target), which need only a ranked list of what is tradeable, and which the roadmap's present stack 05 would and would not satisfy. review2 counts "zero lines of code" against three clauses; check its clause-by-clause table yourself.

THE QUESTIONS YOU MUST ANSWER.
1. **The conditional-versus-unconditional trap.** Both reviews warn: "model minus market equals edge" is wrong when the model's number assumes the hypothesis is true and the market's quote spans every outcome. State the rule that makes the comparison honest, in one sentence, and the smallest data shape that enforces it (so the wrong comparison cannot be typed, in the spirit of "the schema makes the wrong answer impossible").
2. **What a stop-loss honestly is here.** The roadmap derives it from a sensitivity sweep (the claim whose flip hurts an ending most, filtered to claims that resolve earlier and are publicly observable — INV-14). review/ says a sweep can suggest what to WATCH but cannot derive a guaranteed stop, and separates four things: thesis invalidation, offsetting shock, risk exit, execution instruction. review2 wants price paths and first-touch probabilities of a stop and a target, plus an inverse query ("which events take me out?") ranked by lift. Which of these is the smallest thing that is both honest and impressive to a Catalyst reader, and what does each need from the engine (event TIMES per world? a price path? only endpoint worlds?) — coordinate your assumption with the fact that the engine itself may be reformulated (the common brief; analyst ENGINE is on it — assume Kent's direction: an exact core with a sampler on top, time model kept).
3. **How much finance is enough.** review2's bridge is ~650 server lines and ~600 browser lines over three sessions: Quantity/Impact, daily price paths, Position lens, lift, shocks, edge, sizing by quartered Kelly, the card. review/ says: defer expected shortfall, ruin probabilities, automatic sizing and portfolio risk; a conditional thesis with an honest "no positive edge at this price" or "missing quote" is a complete result. Propose the ladder: **the smallest complete stack 05** (what must exist for the brief's trade clauses to be honestly met on the Hormuz map with no key), then each further rung with its cost and what it buys. Be concrete about which rungs you would cut and why.
4. **Outside data with no key.** Polymarket needs no key; FRED needs a free one; continuous integration has none, and the demo must run from a fresh clone with no key. What is recorded, what is fetched live, how a recorded quote is dated on screen, and what the card says when a quote is missing.
5. **The Hormuz fixture's own numbers against reality** — audit-E checked them; say which matter (review2: the OPEC+ prior contradicts its own criteria; the showcase strike should move the quoted instrument by tens of points, not four; delete the `.61 vs .48` prose).
6. **The export** — a declarative document. What fields, and what it must refuse to claim (no guaranteed stop, no execution).
7. **What in the ALREADY-MERGED work must change for your design**, weighed against Kent's high bar: payoffs two-sided? a `Quantity` kind of ending? Does the payoff `kind` fix now in flight (making the discriminator required) conflict with anything you propose? — it changes the prompt's answer shapes and therefore forces a paid re-recording, so if you foresee ANOTHER change to the proposal shapes in stack 05, say so now: it is far cheaper to change them once.

Then write stack 05 as a plan a coordinator could execute: the pull requests in order (at most four deep), what each contains, the shapes as code, the pre-decisions, a checkable "done when", and the decision records it needs (next free number is 0016).

Scratch: `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/b70a1857-a894-4bbe-b3a6-4d7cf3ebc4f8/scratchpad/digest/finance/`. Write your report to `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/analysis/2026-09-21-digest-finance.md` in the common shape (your §2 may run to 1 800 words because it carries the stack plan). Your final message: the 300-word summary.

input.prompt:
You are digest analyst GENERATION. Read `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/briefs/05-review-digest-common.md` first, fully — it is your brief's first half and it binds you. Your lens: **how the model draws a map, what evidence it attaches, and how we know a map is any good.**

YOUR READING (beyond the common list): `plans/review2/audit-G-generation.md`, `plans/review2/research-A-probability-epistemics.md` (the parts on eliciting numbers from a language model: conditionals not joints, base rate first, small ensembles, geometric mean of odds), `plans/review2/research-C-product-landscape.md`; `plans/review/08-engineering-product-audit.md` (generation, evidence, latency), `plans/review/00-final-proposal.md` ("Evidence and testing should challenge the model"), `plans/review/10-proposed-change-plan.md` (generation and evaluation parts), `plans/review/05-concept-and-model-review.md`. Then what exists TODAY — and much has changed since the reviewers looked, so check everything: `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/src/katalyst/engine/` (7 269 lines: `proposal.py`, `prompt.py`, `expand.py` and its split modules, `following.py` the one walk-driver, `grounding.py`, `record.py`, `replay.py`, `client.py`), decision records 0003, 0006 (with its dated amendments), 0012, 0015, `spec/generation/*.md`, `docs/measurements.md`, Kent's decisions G1–G13 in `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/notes/2026-09-17-kent-decisions-stack-04.md`; the one real recording at `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/feat-04b-recordings/backend/recordings/hormuz.jsonl` (29 calls, 93 searches, $4.04, 36 minutes, 18 claims, 19 arrows, 3 refusals) and the kept runs under `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/.runs/`; and the evals on `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/feat-04b-evals` (`evals/`, `spec/generation/evaluation.md`).

MEASURE, DON'T ASSERT. From the real recording and the kept runs, compute with a small script: is the map a pure tree (every claim exactly one parent)? how many cross-links, how many arrows that push DOWN (inhibitors), how many claims that would falsify an ending, depth, the share of claims that are endings, how many base rates kept and how thin (`0/1`, `1/2`), seconds to the FIRST accepted claim and to a first complete chain from hypothesis to an ending (both reviews say: measure time to first useful output, not total time). review2 claims `ClaimProposal`'s single `cause` field is WHY the map is a tree — but a `LinkProposal` shape exists for arrows between existing claims; find out how often the walk actually asks for or gets one.

THE QUESTIONS YOU MUST ANSWER.
1. **Kent's direction for generation is: conditional elicitation, skeleton-first, a small ensemble for numbers** (the common brief). This partly reverses his own earlier decisions — G1/record 0015 (no ensemble), record 0006 (one proposal per call), G7 (up to 25 searches per claim), G4 (three silent retries). For each element, say what the cheapest faithful version is, what it costs (sessions, lines, dollars per map, seconds to first tile and to a finished map), which records it amends, and what it would do to the things that already work and that Kent prizes: reject-never-repair, every refusal visible as an event, provenance decided by us from what the search tool actually returned, the recording/replay format, the one walk-driver. review2's sketch: one streamed structured call drafts the whole DAG (multi-parent, at least one inhibitor and one falsifier per tradeable ending), per-element accept/refuse events ("one DECISION per proposal" instead of "one CALL per proposal"), parallel enrichment per edge on the cheaper model, k = 5 samples per number with the geometric mean of odds, one red-team call; ~3 minutes and ~$0.70 a map. Is that estimate credible against the measured $0.13–0.19 and 27–200 seconds per call? Does a whole-map draft collide with PRD anti-pattern 2 ("never re-prompt for a whole map") or only seem to?
2. **If the engine moves to conditional numbers** (`q0 = P(B | not A)`, `q1 = P(B | A)` per arrow instead of a log-odds strength; analyst ENGINE is weighing it) — what changes in `proposal.py`, the prompt and the validator, and is it cheap to make the proposal shapes ready for it NOW? This matters today: a fix in flight (making the payoff `kind` required) already changes the answer shapes, which moves the prompt fingerprint and forces a paid re-recording of Hormuz (~$4, ~40 minutes). **If stack 05 or 06 will change the shapes again, say so, and say whether the Hormuz re-recording should simply WAIT for that** rather than be paid for twice. Kent has limited recordings to Hormuz and is concerned about how long paid runs take.
3. **Evidence that means something.** review/: a returned URL proves only that the page appeared in a search, not that it supports the probability, the timing or the instrument; attach a passage or locator, its role, and why it is relevant; check the trade-critical sources of the showcase by hand. What is the smallest change to `SourceDraft`/`Source` and the Inspector that gets most of this, and does it belong in stack 05 (grounding) or later?
4. **Evaluation.** Today: four structural cases and a scorecard (unmerged). Both reviews want a small content rubric (8–12 cases: resolvable? mechanism specific? source supports the claim? DAG not tree? priced-in? observation versus intervention?). Who grades — a person, a model, both — what it costs per round, and where it goes (stack 07 has the pastcast; is a rubric better value than a pastcast?).
5. **Use case 1 ("is A → B reasonable?") as a real search** — forward from A and backward from B — against today's Verify door.
6. **The interactive verbs** — add an event, expand this claim, challenge this arrow — against the roadmap's stack 06 (`refine` with its adds-back-up invariant INV-10, role-played experts, a random-simulation probe, feedback-loop unrolling). review2 says cut `refine`, reflexive loops and probes from version one. What of stack 06 survives, and what is it now FOR?

Then write the generation parts of stacks 05–07 as a plan: what is done, in what order, in which stack, with costs; and what is explicitly NOT done and why.

Scratch: `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/b70a1857-a894-4bbe-b3a6-4d7cf3ebc4f8/scratchpad/digest/generation/`. Write your report to `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/analysis/2026-09-21-digest-generation.md` in the common shape. Your final message: the 300-word summary.

input.prompt:
You are digest analyst CRAFT. Read `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/briefs/05-review-digest-common.md` first, fully — it is your brief's first half and it binds you. Your lens: **the interface a reviewer actually meets, the engineering around it, and the process that builds it.**

YOUR READING (beyond the common list): `plans/review2/audit-H-ux-frontend.md` and the five frames in `plans/review2/screenshots/` (look at them — you can read images), `plans/review2/audit-F-engineering-process.md`, `plans/review2/research-C-product-landscape.md`; `plans/review/08-engineering-product-audit.md`, `plans/review/04-independent-product.md`, `plans/review/10-proposed-change-plan.md`, `plans/review/01-independent-first-pass.md`. Then what exists TODAY: `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/frontend/src/` on `main` (15 900 lines) and, more to the point, the growing-map branch at `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/feat-04a-growth/frontend/src/` (reviewed twice, about to land — audit-H ran an EARLIER state of this branch, so re-check each of its findings against the branch's present code: the Inspector, the dock, the panel's scrolling and its "more above / below" rules, `App.tsx`, the stage's edge rule); `spec/workbench/README.md` (the twelve-line visual review checklist), `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §7 (UX-1 to UX-14); `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/HANDOFF.md` (the process as practised), `docs/adr/0009` (stacked pull requests), `docs/adr/0011` (the spec is a book; living architecture), `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, the `Makefile`, `docker/`. Sizes measured today, for your arithmetic: `spec/` is 139 000 words; `backend/src/katalyst/domain` 6 100 lines, `engine` 7 300; `frontend/src` 15 900 lines without tests; `plans/STATUS.md` is 600 lines. You cannot run the browser (the machine is shared and end-to-end runs are the coordinator's); judge from code, component tests and the screenshots, and say so.

THE QUESTIONS YOU MUST ANSWER.
1. **The interface fixes that decide whether the demo happens.** review2's four: a *Change this claim* button group at the top of the Inspector so the brief's core interaction is reachable by mouse (it says it is keyboard-only behind `e` — verify on the growth branch: there IS a "Change this" list in the dock); the right panel scrolls instead of clipping, with the ranked change list on top when a branch is open; end-to-end runs at 1440 × 900 and 1280 × 800 as well as 1600 × 1000; guess-before-reveal on an ending (ask the reader's number, then show the model's — it fills the `user` belief slot the tiles already reserve). For each: still true today? cost? where does it land — the stack-04 tail, or a small polish pull request before stack 05? Also the taste items: `36%` beside `.36` for a trading audience; build and seed provenance moving from the footer to *Run details*. And hold every proposal against Kent's first veto: nothing may look like a template (no dialogs, no spinner-then-dump, density and deliberate detail wanted).
2. **Where the thesis lives on screen (stack 05).** A dock that is always visible and live; the card; *what carries it · what takes you out · what to watch*; how it coexists with the Inspector and the change list on a 1280-wide screen without clipping. Analyst FINANCE owns WHAT the thesis says; you own where it sits and what must move to make room. A sketch in words or an ASCII frame is enough.
3. **The process, weighed honestly.** review2 says the process produced real quality but now spends a quarter of all effort on reconciliation: freeze `spec/` ("the code and its docstrings are the specification from here"), adopt one rule — *no document contains a number the engine computes; prose names the test or the command that prints it* —, merge PRD + ARCHITECTURE into one ten-minute `DESIGN.md`, collapse `plans/` to a `PLAN.md` and an append-only `STATUS.md`, one branch at a time, at most two code-writing agents, keep the read-only reviewer before every pull request, drop stacked pull requests and the async-merge script. Kent, for his part, has said what he values: rigorously documented decisions, a well-structured repository, and a project "principled and simple as possible to understand and maintain" — and his AGENTS.md makes decision records and specs first-class. So do not simply adopt or dismiss: **find the version of each proposal that a maintainer would thank us for.** For instance: is the right move to freeze the spec, or to SHRINK it (which chapters are read by nobody and restate the code; which carry decisions no code can carry)? What does the number rule cost to adopt — analyst XD on another branch is, right now, inventorying every engine-computed number quoted in a committed document; assume about a hundred — and what mechanism makes it cheap (a `make numbers` command whose output a chapter links to? a doctest that fails when a quoted number drifts?)? Which of these is a decision for Kent because it reverses record 0011 or 0009?
4. **Continuous integration and the definition of done.** review2: a numerical oracle as a required check; ONE keyless six-step end-to-end test on the replayed Hormuz map at two viewports, which IS the definition of done; a grep-lint for engine-computed numbers in prose; a latency budget on `/api/worlds`. Today there are six jobs. What is the simplest honest set? Rewrite the project's "definition of done" (it is at the end of `plans/roadmap-03-to-06.md`) around the brief's clauses and a walk a stranger can do with no key — keeping what is already ticked.
5. **Code health, against a high bar.** `App.tsx` was 1 524 lines and is coming down; `propagation.py` is 1 831 lines; docstrings are long by house rule. Both reviews call the craft high and argue against a rewrite. Name at most FIVE refactors of merged code that clear Kent's bar (a clear gain in how fast a stranger understands the code, for bounded work), each with its cost — and say which tempting ones do NOT clear it.
6. **Stack 07 ("make it presentable")** — README walkthrough, a pastcast self-test, an accessibility sweep, a "what I would do next" page. What stays, what moves earlier, what goes.

Then write, as a plan: a small **polish pull request** (if you recommend one) with its contents; the browser half of stack 05; the process and documentation changes as a dated proposal Kent can accept line by line; the new definition of done.

Scratch: `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/b70a1857-a894-4bbe-b3a6-4d7cf3ebc4f8/scratchpad/digest/ux/`. Write your report to `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/analysis/2026-09-21-digest-craft.md` in the common shape. Your final message: the 300-word summary.

input.summary: CRAFT: Kent's correction on spec length
input.message:
Correction from Kent himself (2026-09-21, in chat), which overrides the framing in your brief's question 3: "Please disregard the spec as compression principle as a strict maxim. Instead we can find opportunities to simplify and reduce the length of the specs where warranted."

So: do NOT argue from "the spec must be smaller than the code", do not treat the 139 000-word figure as a defect in itself, and do not recommend freezing `spec/` or replacing it with docstrings. The spec stays a first-class, living book, and chapters-before-code stays the working rule unless you find a specific, local reason otherwise. What Kent wants from you on this point is narrower and more useful: **name the specific places where the spec can be made simpler or shorter with a clear gain** — for example a passage that restates code line by line and carries no decision; the same rule stated in three chapters where one could own it and the others point; worked numbers repeated across chapters (where one owning table, or a command that prints them, would end the re-sweeping); history that belongs in a decision record rather than a book chapter; open-question sections already answered. For each: the chapter, roughly how many words go, what is gained, and the cost. A short ranked list beats a policy.

The number rule ("no document contains a number the engine computes") is still worth weighing on its merits — as a way to stop re-sweeping chapters every time the engine changes — but weigh it as a targeted simplification, and offer the gentler variant too: ONE owning place for the worked example's numbers, generated by a command and checked in CI, that every chapter points to.

Everything else in your brief stands.

input.description: Wire fix: one-rule redesign
input.prompt:
You are agent J2, one Opus sub-agent finishing stack 04 of the Katalyst project. You take over the branch `fix/04-vanishing-wire` from agent J after its independent review.

Read first, fully, in this order:
1. /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/briefs/04-common.md  (binding)
2. /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/briefs/04-resume-common.md  (binding — the machine's resource rules: you NEVER run `npx playwright test` in any form; the coordinator runs every browser end-to-end run and every repeat bar)
3. /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/RESUME-stack-04.md — section "4. fix/04-vanishing-wire".
4. In the worktree: AGENTS.md; `git show HEAD` (the one commit, 6bc90d3); frontend/src/graph/Canvas.tsx; frontend/src/graph/toFlow.ts and frontend/src/graph/__tests__/measured.test.ts (how #37 declares each tile's box); frontend/src/components/tile.css around the port rules (about lines 470–500); spec/workbench/tiles-ports-wires.md "The ports" and spec/workbench/layout-and-zoom.md (it says layout is "never measured off the screen — so layout stays a pure function").

WORKTREE: /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst-wt/fix-04-vanishing-wire , branch fix/04-vanishing-wire, one commit on main (48eb562). You are alone in it; you may commit (Conventional Commits, co-author line). Do not push.

THE STORY SO FAR. About once in 200 loaded runs a wire between two tiles was never drawn while every tile was in place. J showed the cause: the drawing library (@xyflow/react 12.11.6) draws a wire between two HANDLES (the project's word is PORT — spec/vocabulary.md); where a port sits is measured through a browser size notification that a busy browser can drop; #37 had declared each tile's BOX to the library (`initialWidth`/`initialHeight` in toFlow.ts) so tiles survive a dropped notification, but not its ports. J's fix: a hook `useHandlesTheLibraryHasMeasured` that asks the library to re-measure every 120 ms "until it says every node is initialised". The coordinator ran the last bar on it: 600 of 600 end-to-end runs green at 1, 3 and 6 workers.

48	## 2. The design I recommend
49	
50	### 2.1 The rule that makes the comparison honest
51	
52	> **A model number may be differenced against a market quote only when both range over the same set of worlds — so the edge is computed from the world with *no supposition in force*, and a supposed world can only ever show a conditional payoff.**
53	
54	The smallest shape that enforces it is a **signature, not a guard**. The edge is never computed from "a world"; it is computed by one function that requires the base world as its own argument:
55	
56	```python
57	# katalyst/thesis/edge.py — outside domain/, because it touches a quote (INV-11, ADR-0003)
58	
59	class Quote(BaseModel):                     # what a venue says. Never merged with a model number.
60	    venue: str; contract_id: str
61	    p: float                                # the mid, as a probability
62	    spread: float                           # best offer minus best bid
63	    as_of: date; url: str
64	    source: Literal["fetched", "recorded", "user"]
65	
66	class Edge(BaseModel):                      # built by `priced()` and nowhere else
67	    model: Belief                           # unconditional, owner='model'
68	    quote: Quote
69	    costs: float                            # half the spread plus fees, as a probability
70	    edge: float                             # model.p − quote.p − costs. Signed. May be negative.
71	    break_even: float                       # quote.p + costs — useful even with no quote
72	    mixture: tuple[MixtureTerm, ...]        # every term shown: P(H)·P(c|do H) + (1−P(H))·P(c|do ¬H)
73	
74	class NotComparable(BaseModel):
75	    reason: Literal["conditional_world", "no_quote", "no_contract", "different_question"]
76	    said: str                               # the plain sentence the card prints
77	    break_even: float | None                # still printable when only the quote is missing
78	
79	def priced(base: World, shown: World, claim: PropositionId, quote: Quote | None) -> Edge | NotComparable: ...
80	```
81	
82	`base` and `shown` are two required arguments; there is no way to hand `priced` a branch world alone, and `Edge` has no other construction path. Tests: *agree with the market ⇒ edge reads exactly 0*; *a branch world alone does not type-check*; *a missing quote yields `NotComparable` that still prints the break-even.*
83	
84	The **mixture** is the piece both reviews wanted and neither costed: after *Suppose Hormuz opens*, the card still says *"your supposition makes M1 .61; weighted by the map's own P(H) = .36 against the no-open world's .40, the unconditional number is .47 — that is the one compared with .48."* review/'s worked example, with the engine supplying the terms. It needs only `do(¬A)`, which exists.

86	### 2.2 What a stop-loss honestly is here
87	
88	Four things, kept apart on the card, three of them named differently from today:
89	
90	| Card section | What it is | Who owns it | How it is computed |
91	|---|---|---|---|
92	| **What takes you out** | The events over-represented in the worlds where the stop was touched **first** | computed | `lift(k) = P(k happened before the stop ∣ stop first) / P(k happened)`, Wilson interval on the numerator, suppressed below 200 draws, with the median days between *k* and the stop |
93	| **What to watch** | The claim whose adverse flip hurts the terminal most, **and** resolves before it, **and** is publicly observable | computed | two-directional `sensitivity()` + INV-14's two filters. *Renamed from "invalidation"; it is a watchlist, not a stop.* |
94	| **Your risk exit** | The stop price, the target, the horizon | **the user types them** | never derived |
95	| **Execution** | — | — | We say one sentence: *a stop order's trigger is not its fill price*, and nothing else. |
96	
97	**The smallest thing that is both honest and impressive is "what takes you out".** Forty lines over a boolean mask; the brief's most distinctive sentence answered by computation rather than prose; the one output nobody in the competitive landscape ships. "What to watch" is fifteen lines and is the honest remnant of INV-14. Everything above them — expected shortfall, ruin, drawdown — is cut.
98	
99	**What each needs from the engine.** Only one thing, and it is small:
100	
101	```python
102	# katalyst/thesis/draws.py — the ONLY coupling between the finance layer and the engine
103	class Draws(BaseModel):
104	    day_zero: date; days: int
105	    order: tuple[PropositionId, ...]
106	    when:   NDArray[int]      # (n, claims): the day each claim first became true, −1 for never
107	    weight: NDArray[float]    # (n,): all ones for an exact ancestral sampler
108	```
109	
110	"What to watch" needs **endpoint marginals only** — today's `sensitivity()` gives them. P(stop first) / P(target first) need **event times per world**. The inverse query needs **joint samples with times**. All three come from `when`.
111	
112	`weight` is in the shape from day one so the finance layer is **indifferent to ENGINE's Plan A versus Plan B**: an exact core with an ancestral sampler gives weights of one, a likelihood-weighted sampler gives real weights, and nothing above changes. And `when` is derivable from *today's* engine too — `_draw` already computes `truth[claim] = came_true`, a `(versions, worlds, days)` boolean array, whose first true day **is** `when`. **So stack 05 is not blocked on the engine reformulation**: write it against synthetic `Draws`, test it against synthetic `Draws`, turn it on over whichever engine lands.

94	## 2. The design I recommend
95	
96	**One sentence: freeze the answer shapes once, record once, buy the latency cheaply, and make
97	skeleton-first a measured bet in stack 06 rather than an article of faith.**
98	
99	### 2.1 The shape freeze (stack 05, top)
100	
101	Everything that changes `STANDING_TEXT` or `what_goes_out()` moves the prompt fingerprint
102	(`prompt.py:154`), and a moved fingerprint fails `check_recordings` and costs a paid re-record
103	(~$4, ~40 min) plus a cassette re-record (~$1). So they go in **one commit, once**:
104	
105	```python
106	class LinkDraft(BaseModel):
107	    mode: Literal["trigger", "sustain"]
108	    p_effect_if_cause: float      # P(effect | cause), plain probability
109	    p_effect_if_not_cause: float  # P(effect | not cause)
110	    lag: int
111	    shape: Literal["impulse", "step", "ramp"]
112	    half_life: int | None = None
113	    rationale: str
114	    what_would_change_my_mind: str     # one named observable
115	    sources: tuple[SourceDraft, ...] = ()
116	
117	class SourceDraft(BaseModel):
118	    url: str
119	    quote: str   # the sentence on that page that carries the weight
120	    role: Literal["mechanism", "magnitude", "timing", "resolution", "instrument"]
121	```
122	
123	Our code keeps every decision it already owns: it mints ids, stamps `owner="model"`, computes
124	`strength = logit(q₁) − logit(q₀)` (clipped, with the clip reported), sets the leak to `q₀`, decides
125	`documented`/`argued` from what the search returned, and now also records whether the quote's page was
126	reachable. **Removed**: `strength` as an elicited field, and with it the "+1 triples the odds" anchor.
127	Also in the freeze: `kind` required on both payoff shapes (the branch already written); the three
128	inhibitor/falsifier sentences; the "do not search on the first call" rule; the thin-base-rate rule.
129	
130	**Then, and only then, re-record Hormuz once.** Everything else waits behind it.
131	
132	### 2.2 Latency, bought cheaply
133	
134	Two changes, measured, ~40 lines: the starting call does not search (**7 s** to the first tile,
135	measured) and `at_once` goes 3 → 5 (measured parallelism is already 1.5× at 3). At `EFFORT=medium`
136	that is a first tile at ~15 s and a whole map in ~5 minutes for $1.31 — which is what a live user
137	gets. The recordings stay at default effort (G13 stands).
138	
139	### 2.3 Skeleton-first: a bet, not a premise (stack 06)
140	
141	Its quality argument is measurably dead — the walk already draws DAGs with up to four parents. Its
142	remaining case is **more map per minute** and a first tile that arrives while a human is still
143	reading the hypothesis. Priced against the measurements, not the sketch: **≈$2.0–2.6 and ≈5–6
144	minutes** for 15–18 claims, first tile ~20 s *and only if we build a streaming JSON path that does
145	not exist today*. Compare: today's medium-effort run with §2.2's fixes is ~5 minutes and $1.31 for
146	9–12 claims. So it buys size and first-paint, not wall clock, for about twice the money and 2.5–3
147	sessions.
148	
149	Build it as **one decision per proposal, with proposals arriving in batches** — `grow.py` stays the
150	one walk driver, each element in the skeleton folds through the same `_judge` on the same candidate
151	map, and each emits the same `proposal_accepted` / `proposal_rejected` with a rising `at`, so the
152	recording grammar, replay and reject-never-repair all survive untouched. Amends ADR-0006's *"one
153	call per proposal"* to *"one decision per proposal"*. **Kill criterion, decided on the scorecard:**
154	if a skeleton round does not beat the walk on `claims`, `inhibiting_links` and `source_support_rate`
155	at equal or lower dollars, it is deleted and the walk stands.
156	
157	### 2.4 Evidence (stack 05, with the fetch-check in 06)
158	
159	The smallest change that gets most of the value is the two fields above plus an Inspector that reads
160	*quote → role → link*, and **the showcase's trade-critical sources checked by hand once** — which is
161	what both reviews actually ask for. Review2's automatic check cannot be built: the service returns
162	`encrypted_content`, not text, and the structured answer carries no `citations`. The honest automatic
163	version is **our own** fetch of the cited page and a substring match — the same shape of rule as
164	`keep_cited`, and a fourth word a reader can trust. It belongs in 06 because it adds a network step
165	to generation that replay must never need.
166	
167	### 2.5 Evaluation (counts in 05, rubric in 07)
168	
169	Add the seven counting columns to the existing scorecard — they cost nothing and they are exactly the
170	properties that changed between 09-17 and today, so they are what a regression would show. Keep the
171	house rule that **no model grades a model**. The content questions both reviews want are graded by
172	**a person, once per round**, on a printed sheet of 10 maps × 6 axes: resolvable · mechanism specific
173	· source supports the claim · DAG not tree · priced-in named · observation versus intervention. One
174	afternoon. Put it in stack 07 beside the pastcast — and **prefer the rubric to the pastcast**: the
175	pastcast needs a date-frozen corpus we do not have, and review/ 10:31 warns that a binary Brier score
176	cannot validate an interval over a latent probability anyway. The rubric is the cheaper instrument
177	and it answers the question Kent actually has.
178	
179	### 2.6 Interactive verbs (stack 06) — and what stack 06 is now FOR
180	
181	Stack 06 stops being "probes" and becomes **the map you can argue with**: *expand this claim* ·
182	*challenge this arrow* · *add an event* (built, one live run from proven), ranked by *spend here*
183	(already computed). *Challenge this arrow* **is** the role-played expert FR-9 permits and the red-team
184	call review2 wants — one feature where the roadmap had two. Cut: `refine`/INV-10, reflexive-loop
185	unrolling, the random-simulation probe.
186	
187	**Records amended:** ADR-0006 (one *decision* per proposal; the research budget narrowed), ADR-0003's
188	2026-09-17 amendment (unchanged — three silent retries stand), ADR-0015 (the coherence residual now;
189	k = 3 only if the scorecard earns it; G1's *"nothing extra in a recording"* is what an ensemble would
190	break, and it must be said out loud), ADR-0010 (a source carries a passage and a role), ADR-0013
191	(`kind` required). PRD anti-pattern 2 gains one clarifying clause.

**1. `observe(B=true)` leaves a cause at its prior (.3000 against Bayes's .4562).** Root cause: step 3 of `propagation.md` B5 — *keep the likelihood, not the coin flip*. `_one_pass` keeps `answer` (the claim's marginal likelihood in that draw) and throws away `came_true` (the realised flag). For a claim with **no causes** `total` is `broadcast(baseline)`, so `answer` is *identical in all eight worlds of a version*; `_per_version` then averages it over the surviving subset and gets exactly the same number back. Rao-Blackwellisation is exact for an *unconditional* mean, and invalid once you condition on another claim's realised outcome, because the conditioning event depends on the value that was discarded. The Bayes answer would come back by reading `came_true[A]` over the surviving worlds instead of `answer[A]`, at the cost of the variance reduction the whole band rests on — which is why this is a design decision and not a patch. It is the same phenomenon `diff.md` already records as G3's "moved only by reweighting", described there as a property rather than as a defect. **Interaction with the spread: none.** A has no incoming arrows, so no drawn push enters its baseline and its answer is still constant across worlds within a version. For a claim that *does* have causes, the answer already varies across worlds, the observation does reach it, and the spread only widens the band.

The two readings that would let later pushes through are "the day this arrow's own push fires" (`settled[source] + lag`) and "the source's own resolve-by day"; both change every recorded number, so this is Kent's call. **Interaction with the spread: none that can change the zero.** The spread varies `H→B`, `C→B` and `R→B`, so it changes the distribution of B's day-2 flag — but identically in the base world and the `do(C)` world, because C's arrow contributes nothing on day 2 in either. Three of the four analyst reports are in. The interface-and-process report tested every claim in the second review's interface audit against the growth branch as it stands now, and most of those findings no longer hold.

- **Six of that audit's findings are already fixed on the growth branch.**
  - The panel scrolls as one and marks where more lies beyond each edge.
  - `App.tsx` is down from 1,524 lines to 483.
  - Fitting the view to the map accounts for the panel.
  - `engineState` is memoized, so the map no longer re-routes on every keystroke.
  - There is an error boundary.
  - There is a light theme.
- **One finding that would stop the demo is still true: the six operations can't be reached with the mouse.** They open only with the `e` key or the command palette. A button in the Inspector is about 20 lines. That leads a nine-item polish pull request of about three hours, all in the browser.
- **On the spec, it took your correction and found eight local cuts with no freeze.** Together they remove about 24,500 words, roughly 17%. The largest comes from one line of the chapter template. That line asks for the pydantic models verbatim in each Data model section, and it accounts for about 43,000 words, which already duplicate the code 50–79%. The proposed change is to state the shape and name the module that defines it.
- **The visual review checklist is cited 35 times by line number, and `ARCHITECTURE.md` miscounts its lines.** Citing the checklist lines by name fixes that.
- **It rejected several proposals and gave reasons.**
  - A probability slider would write thirty edits into an append-only audit trail.
  - Screenshot baselines would be flaky tests.
  - Merging the PRD and `ARCHITECTURE.md` does not fix drift. A 40-line test of the built/planned markers does.
  - `propagation.py` is 812 lines of code under long docstrings, so splitting it is not worth it.
- **The thesis needs no new room on screen.** It fits as a pinned three-line strip above the panel. The "what takes you out" list is the existing change-list component run backwards.

The engine report is the one still outstanding, and it decides the most. It settles whether the spread lands and what the engine work is before the thesis. When it arrives I'll synthesise all four, have the plan attacked once, and write the planning docs.

**Summary**

Both defects reproduce on `48eb562`, and I found a third: a claim with prior `.001` carrying a `−0.01` arrow **voids a supposition on day zero** — the tile never reads *Supposed*. Root causes are `propagation.py:1470-1472` (V1: a Rao-Blackwellised estimate averaged over surviving worlds is constant for a non-descendant of the evidence) and `_settled_days:806-843` + `:1463` (V2: one integer does two jobs — when outgoing delays start counting, and when a claim's truth is decided).

Three measurements decided the recommendation. **review2's Plan A is ~1000× more expensive than its own estimate**: on generated 20-claim maps with in-degree 3, exact elimination over event times costs 0.7–7.8 s per band at K=12 with 4.8M–62.7M-entry intermediates (it predicted ≲10⁶ and "milliseconds"); 58–119 s at 30 claims. Its own kill criterion fires at K=6. But **the same network over binary truths, with all 200 versions on one numpy axis, is 0.5 ms** — the whole band, one pass.

So: **keep review2's hazard model exactly; stop making event time a variable the network solves for.** The arrow keeps `strength`/`mode`/`lag`/`shape`/`half_life` as a hazard modifier; each parent's arrival time comes from one forward pass (redone under a `do`), not from inference; the binary network is solved exactly by variable elimination. Measured cost of that collapse against Plan A's exact answer: worst 0.0065 on a multi-parent map; over 30 generated maps with inhibitors, 97% of numbers within 0.01. Three sessions, net −350 lines in `propagation.py`, staged so `main` is never red (new core behind `engine="exact"`, then one flag flip). Locality becomes a theorem; the band becomes exact; V1, V2, starvation, the clamp bias and observe-noise all die together.

Also: **land the spread** (it rides the versions, not the nest); **cut the path product** — it never moved to `domain/`, it is at `verify.py:139-167` — and replace it at 05 with total effect + joint + weakest arrow, rewriting INV-8; **recommend the event/state split** (net *negative* lines, reverses ADR-0014 A — Kent's call); **reject** moving formatting out of `domain/`, fix three raw-`repr` sites instead; and land `make numbers` + a committed `worked-numbers.txt` **before** the core change, since 547 prose decimals die with it.</result>

100	## 2. The design I recommend
101	
102	**One sentence: keep review2's hazard model exactly, and stop making event time a variable
103	the network has to solve for.**
104	
105	### What a claim means
106	
107	A claim is a resolvable proposition with a deadline `D`, and its number is
108	`P(it resolves YES by D)` — a first-passage probability, which is what the sentence on the
109	tile already says. It is not an instantaneous state probability read on a deadline, and it
110	can never un-resolve.
111	
112	### Where the time model lives
113	
114	On the edge, unchanged in vocabulary. Every arrow keeps `strength`, `mode`, `lag`, `shape`,
115	`half_life`; they now modify a **hazard** — the rate at which a claim happens on a given day —
116	instead of a log-odds read on one day:
117	
118	```
119	λ_i(t) = λ⁰_i · exp( Σ_j  w_ij · shape_ij(t − τ_j − lag_ij) )
120	P(i by D_i | parents) = 1 − exp( −∫₀^{D_i} λ_i(t) dt )
121	```
122	
123	`λ⁰` comes from the claim's own `prior`, which is honestly the leak — `q₀ = P(i by D | no
124	modelled cause)` — and the edge weight from `q₁ = P(i by D | this cause happened)`, both in
125	closed form (review2 `03` §1.3). The integral is exact per piecewise-constant segment, so it
126	is grid-independent **provided every breakpoint is on the grid** — which is exactly what
127	`_prepare`'s `must_be_exact` set already guarantees, and it is what keeps the #38 locality
128	proof alive. An impulse's whole area now counts, so the answer no longer depends on where
129	the deadline falls relative to the half-life; that is E5 and ADR-0014's admitted wart, gone.
130	
131	### Where the parent's arrival time comes from
132	
133	**One forward pass, not inference.** Each claim's own first-passage distribution over a
134	coarse grid (K ≈ 12–24 epochs) is computed once, causes first, in `O(n·K·2^indegree)`; a
135	`do` recomputes it with that claim pinned to the day it was supposed. A child's conditional
136	table is then the hazard integral averaged over its parents' arrival distributions.
137	
138	That is the entire idea, and it is the one thing neither review proposed. Measured cost of
139	the approximation against full exact inference over event times: **worst 0.0065** on a
140	multi-parent map, **97 % of all numbers within 0.01** over 30 generated maps with inhibitors.
141	Measured saving: **0.5 ms against 0.7–7.8 s** for a 20-claim band.
142	
143	### What solves the network
144	
145	The claims are then **binary**, and the joint is solved **exactly** by variable elimination
146	with a min-fill ordering — the 200 parameter versions and the ~180 displayed days carried as
147	leading `numpy` axes, so the whole band is one pass. `do` replaces a factor with a point mass
148	and cuts the arrows in; `observe` multiplies in an indicator and renormalises. Both are
149	exact, which kills E1, E3, E4 and E9 in one change. The band becomes the 10th/90th percentile
150	of 200 exact answers — ADR-0014's *meaning* of the range is untouched; its machinery shrinks
151	to a loop.
152	
153	Two properties fall out rather than being engineered. **Locality becomes a theorem**: a
154	claim d-separated from the evidence gets its prior back bit-for-bit, because its factor sums
155	to one — so `_observation_reach`'s careful per-observation masks stop being a mechanism and
156	become a fact. And **`range_shares` becomes exact**: re-solve with one prior frozen, `n`
157	extra solves at 0.5 ms, instead of a 20-bin estimator over a discarded sample.
158
